evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates whether regulatory control of open currency positions (OCPs) is sufficient to measure the economic foreign exchange risk of a commercial bank and translates the findings into requirements for a digital riskmanagement platform. Official monthly exchange rates of the Central Bank of the Republic of Uzbekistan for January 2020 – September 2025 (69 observations) are used to construct four model portfolios with the same aggregate long OCP equal to 10% of banking-system regulatory capital. Parametric, historical-simulation, and Student-t Monte Carlo VaR estimates are compared; Expected Shortfall, Kupiec backtesting, and five stress scenarios are also applied. Although every portfolio has the same regulatory position ratio, monthly 99% parametric VaR ranges from 0.22% to 1.58% of regulatory capital — a 7.24-fold difference. A 10-day square-root-of-time conversion preserves the disparity, producing estimates of approximately 0.15% – 1.09% of capital. The diversified portfolio's VaR is 44.1% below the sum of standalone currency VaRs, demonstrating information about correlations that the additive OCP measure cannot capture. The article's second contribution is an event-driven platform design in which every accepted exchange-rate update or transaction atomically updates the position ledger, revalues exposures, recalculates OCP, VaR, Expected Shortfall, and stress scenarios, tests both regulatory and internal limits, and stores an auditable snapshot. Manual spreadsheet-based analysis cannot provide the same calculation frequency, data consistency, or traceability. VaR should therefore complement — not replace — OCP limits, while a digital platform converts the 10-day, 99% VaR requirement of paragraph 91¹ of Regulation No. 3427 into a continuous management control.

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the manuscript "Three-dimensional resistivity imaging constrains crustal heterogeneity beneath the 2010 Yushu Ms 7.1 earthquake rupture," accepted for publication in Geophysical Research Letters . The dataset contains processed magnetotelluric (MT) response functions in EDI format and the preferred three-dimensional electrical resistivity model derived from the MT survey conducted after the 2010 Yushu Ms 7.1 earthquake in the eastern Tibetan Plateau. The survey comprised 83 MT sites, of which 70 were retained for the final three-dimensional inversion after quality control. The EDI files contain processed frequency-domain MT responses and associated observational information. The file YSdata.dat contains the preferred three-dimensional resistivity model in a four-column format: Longitude (decimal degrees) Latitude (decimal degrees) Elevation (relative to sea level, unit: km) Log₁₀ electrical resistivity, defined as log₁₀[ρ/(Ω·m)] The fourth column represents the base-10 logarithm of the modeled electrical resistivity, rather than apparent resistivity. Electrical resistivity in Ω·m can be recovered by raising 10 to the power of the fourth-column value. These data support the interpretation of crustal resistivity heterogeneity and its spatial relationship to the rupture and aftershock distribution of the 2010 Yushu earthquake. The original electromagnetic time-series recordings and proprietary inversion source code are not included in this dataset.
evidence_items.title: Magnetotelluric response functions and three-dimensional resistivity model for the 2010 Yushu earthquake, eastern Tibetan Plateau

evidence_items.summary: The exact numerical evaluation of the spatial correlation function $g(r)$ in the $\mathbb{F} 1$ manifold previously yielded a trivial saturation value of $+1.0$. This paper demonstrates that this behavior is not a computational artifact but an exact mathematical consequence of the Kaleidoscopic Filter Theorem. We resolve this anomaly by introducing a parity-based thermodynamic mapping, effectively transitioning from a strictly positive geometric volume to a fluctuating physical observable. This mapping induces massive destructive interference, perfectly counteracting the Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotic growth and revealing the true oscillatory nature of the correlation function, confirming early physical intuitions regarding requisite signal cancellations.
evidence_items.title: Kaleidoscopic Resolution of the Correlation Anomaly: Thermodynamic Parity and Exact Cancellations in the $\mathbb{F}_1$ Manifold

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Hyperacute stent thrombosis is a rare yet life-threatening complication that may develop within minutes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Despite optimal stent deployment and dual antiplatelet therapy, hyperacute stent thrombosis may occur due to procedural, pharmacological and patient-related factors, including underlying genetic and metabolic abnormalities. A 54-year-old man presented with acute anterior STEMI. Coronary angiography demonstrated total occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery and successful primary PCI with stent implantation restored coronary blood flow. Fifteen minutes after the procedure, the patient developed ventricular fibrillation accompanied by vomiting, raising concern for impaired absorption of orally administered antiplatelet therapy. Emergent repeat coronary angiography revealed hyperacute stent thrombosis, which was managed with balloon angioplasty and intracoronary tirofiban administration. During follow-up, recurrent hyperacute stent thrombosis developed, requiring additional stent implantation and continuous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor infusion. Further laboratory evaluation excluded hereditary thrombophilia and autoimmune disorders; however, severe hyperhomocysteinemia associated with a homozygous methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) C677T mutation was identified. Subsequently, B-vitamin supplementation therapy was initiated. This case highlights the multifactorial pathophysiology of hyperacute stent thrombosis and underscores the potential contributory role of MTHFR-associated hyperhomocysteinemia. Early recognition of underlying metabolic abnormalities and prompt initiation of B-vitamin therapy may help reduce the risk of recurrent thrombotic events.
evidence_items.title: Recurrent Hyperacute Stent Thrombosis in STEMI: MTHFR-Related Hyperhomocysteinemia

evidence_items.summary: Asymptomatic adnexal masses detected after menopause present a diagnostic challenge because many are benign, whereas a subset represent borderline or invasive neoplasms. Objective: To synthesize clinically relevant ultrasonographic and tissue-based morphological criteria for malignancy risk stratification, with particular attention to the appropriate role of immunohistochemistry (IHC). Methods: A focused narrative review of published consensus recommendations, ultrasound classification studies, and established principles of ovarian tumor pathology. This is not a systematic review and no patient-level dataset was analyzed. Findings: Standardized transvaginal ultrasonography, including O-RADS and IOTA approaches, supports preoperative risk estimation. Solid components, papillary projections, irregular morphology, ascites, and vascularity warrant structured assessment, but no isolated feature is diagnostic. Histopathology remains central to definitive classification; IHC panels such as PAX8, WT1, p53, p16, Ki-67, Napsin A, and HNF1B may refine subtype assignment when interpreted with morphology. Conclusion: A staged diagnostic pathway combining clinical context, expert imaging, selective biomarkers, and morphology-directed IHC can improve diagnostic consistency. Prospective studies are required to test prediction of future malignant transformation, which cannot be inferred from cross-sectional risk classification.
evidence_items.title: HISTOMORPHOLOGICAL AND IMMUNOHISTOCHEMICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF ASYMPTOMATIC OVARIAN NEOPLASMS IN POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN: CORRELATION WITH ULTRASONOGRAPHIC FEATURES

evidence_items.summary: The Political Violence in Bangladesh (PVB) dataset is a new event dataset covering more than 35,000 incidents of political violence from 1991–2018. Drawing on four national newspapers, the PVB provides unusually fine-grained information on actors, targets, triggers, forms of violence, and human and material impacts. For the most prominent perpetrators of political violence in Bangladesh, the political parties, the PVB distinguishes not only between different parties but also between their student and youth wings and, within these, different types of actors. Because the data capture the full spectrum of Bangladesh’s violent politics beyond election periods, it enables the study of both electoral violence and broader shifts in violent politics as Bangladesh moves from democracy toward electoral autocracy, including changes in perpetrators and targets. By offering detailed yet structured data in a single-country setting, the PVB opens new avenues for theorizing violent politics in democracies and provides a foundation for future cross-country comparisons as similar datasets become available for other contexts.
evidence_items.title: Political Violence in Bangladesh (PVB) dataset

evidence_items.summary: Natural-language assistants can open institutional data warehouses to non-technical staff, but their most harmful failures are silent: a well-formed query that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. We study these errors on an Italian university's live data warehouse, using an on-premises research prototype built on the open-weight Mixture-of-Experts model gpt-oss-120b, and ask whether the model's routing decisions reveal them. We built a benchmark of 1000 Italian questions from 51 templates, with references checked against official reports and semantic conventions recorded explicitly. The assistant answered 70-77% of evaluable questions correctly and returned a silent error on 19-23%; hand-written guards did not reduce silent errors, and many depended on undocumented institutional conventions rather than on the model. From the accepted queries we extracted per-layer router statistics and trained probes validated across question templates. Token-level confidence was at chance (AUROC 0.51), and routing features averaged over layers (0.56) were no better than a control that only recognises the question; kept per layer, routing reached 0.75 and added information to question metadata (0.77 combined). Delivering only the least suspicious half of the answers reduced silent errors from 21% to 10%. Routing signals offer a cheap, internal basis for triaging answers on institutional data. Preprint of a manuscript submitted to Knowledge-Based Systems (Elsevier) on 8 October 2026. Supporting data and code are deposited separately: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23292481
evidence_items.title: Does the Router Know? Mixture-of-Experts Routing Signals for Detecting Silent Errors in Text-to-SQL over University Data Warehouses

evidence_items.summary: The Melghat region of Maharashtra, India, located in the Satpura ranges, harbors a rich diversity of medicinal plants traditionally utilized by tribal communities. Amorphophallus campanulatus (Elephant foot yam) is one such ethnomedicinally important species known for its therapeutic and nutritional value. The present study was undertaken to evaluate the qualitative phytochemical composition of A. campanulatus collected from the Melghat forest region to assess its bioactive potential and suitability for sustainable cultivation. Ethanolic, methanolic, and aqueous extracts of the plant material were subjected to standard phytochemical screening for secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic compounds, tannins, saponins, terpenoids, and cardiac glycosides. The results revealed a strong presence of alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolics, tannins, and terpenoids across all solvent extracts, while saponins and cardiac glycosides were absent. The richness of bioactive compounds suggests significant antioxidant and antimicrobial potential. These findings support the promotion of A. campanulatus for large-scale cultivation in the Melghat region, contributing to biodiversity conservation and enhancing livelihood opportunities for local communities.
evidence_items.title: From Forest to Farm: Phytochemical Evaluation of Amorphophallus campanulatus from the Melghat Region for Sustainable Cultivation and Biodiversity Conservation

evidence_items.summary: Rapid growth in IoT devices has led to the creation of crucial cybersecurity threats since existing methods of malware detection which use signature matching and numerical feature analysis are incapable of capturing the contextual behavioral semantics of IoT attacks. The presented work proposes an innovative malware detection framework incorporating a pipeline of behavior-to-text transformation together with transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform binary classification of IoT network traffic. Selected through the process of SHAP-based feature importance analysis, the numerical features of network flows from the initial set of 41 features are transformed into natural language descriptions, allowing encoder-based LLMs to capture the context of IoT traffic behavior. Four LLMs, including DistilBERT, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa, were fine-tuned and rigorously tested against four Deep Learning baselines, Neural Network, LSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN, and four Machine Learning baselines, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, using the CIC-IoT-2023 dataset under three experimental setups: balanced classification, realistic imbalanced distribution, and unseen variant detection. Additionally, a four-class multi-class classification experiment and an ablation study were conducted to further validate the framework. On a balanced dataset consisting of 400,000 samples, BERT-base and RoBERTa achieved the highest F1-scores of 98.94% with precision above 99.96%. In the imbalanced case of 90% attack and 10% benign traffic, the precision of all models was equal to 99.99%. The framework attained an F1-score of 99.99% for unseen variant detection on a completely unseen Mirai botnet variant with zero false negatives. The four-class multi-class experiment achieved a Macro F1-score of 88.80%. Statistical analysis across three independent runs confirmed high result stability with standard deviations below 0.03%.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can enhance learning engagement and accessibility, though their performance in dentistry is inconsistent. Bitewing radiographs are critical for caries detection but prone to diagnostic errors from operator positioning. This study compared the performance of four LLMs with reasoning capabilities, GPT o1, GPT o3‐mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Grok 3, in generating scenario‐specific educational feedback from a structured textual format of bitewing radiographs. Materials and Methods Ten positioning error scenarios were created by DMFR specialists. LLMs were evaluated using an original prompt (OP) and an engineered prompt (EP), resulting in a 4 × 2 LLM‐by‐prompt design. Each LLM was tested via its model‐specific access mode: API or web interface. Eighty outputs were assessed by two DMFR specialists for detail, content, clarity and relevance using a 5‐point Likert scale. Ordinal category‐level scores were analysed using a cumulative link mixed‐effects model, with LLM, prompt type, scenario group, assessment category and LLM × prompt as fixed effects, and scenario as a random intercept. Results The LLM–prompt interaction was significant, indicating prompt engineering affected models differently. GPT o3‐mini had significantly lower odds of higher scores than Gemini 2.0 Flash, while EP reduced Grok 3 performance. Positioning error type influenced performance, with significant model‐dependent differences across scenario groups. No significant LLM–assessment category interaction was observed, suggesting model differences did not vary across assessment categories. Conclusion LLM‐generated feedback varied by model, prompt design and positioning error type, but not consistently across assessment categories. Outputs require validation, model‐specific prompt testing and specialist review before implementation.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Treatment-related adverse event documentation is labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. We developed and evaluated VOICE-AE, a multi-stage pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization and large language models (LLMs) for automated extraction and grading of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) toxicities from clinician-patient audio recordings. Encounters of prostate cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy were recorded and processed through VOICE-AE. Six blinded human raters independently graded 10 genitourinary/gastrointestinal toxicities from the same transcripts; hierarchical clustering identified an expert-rater subgroup that established the consensus reference standard. A total of 31 patients (39 encounters) were enrolled, yielding 390 encounter–toxicity assessments, of which 300 (76.9%) carried a reference grade of 0. Six-rater Krippendorff alpha was 0.677 for ordinal grading. Against reference standard, VOICE-AE achieved a mean weighted kappa of 0.717 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.669. Exact CTCAE grade match was 82.6% and within-one-grade accuracy 99.2%; because grade 0 predominated, a trivial classifier always predicting grade 0 would achieve 76.9% and 93.6% respectively. Performance was weaker at the grades that drive clinical action (grade 1 F1 0.58; grade 2 F1 0.57), and binary detection sensitivity was 77.8% with specificity 89.0% and precision 68.0%. In a like-for-like comparison restricted to the three expert-cluster raters, mean weighted kappa between VOICE-AE and those experts (0.666) fell just below agreement among the experts themselves (0.681). VOICE-AE performed within the range of inter-expert agreement, supporting the feasibility of automated, post-encounter AE documentation. Accuracy at grade ≥2 and detection of severe toxicity remain unproven.
evidence_items.title: VOICE-AE: automated CTCAE scoring from ambient clinical audio using speech recognition and large language models

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in patient education. This study evaluated the responses of AI chatbots to frequently asked questions about osteoporosis in Turkish in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate AI-generated responses to osteoporosis-related questions in Turkish.Materials and methods: Thirty-one of the most common frequently asked questions related to osteoporosis were subcategorized into general information, diagnosis, and treatment. The questions were submitted to the publicly accessible platforms ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity. Two physicians evaluated accuracy (six-point Likert scale) and completeness (three-point Likert scale) based on the 2025 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Osteoporosis and Metabolic Bone Diseases. Readability was assessed using the Ateşman Readability Formula.Results: No significant difference was found among the chatbots for accuracy. Accuracy rates ranged 80.5%-82.2% overall, 82.3%-85.2% general information, 58.3%-66.7% diagnosis, and 77.2%-81.7% treatment. Significant differences were found in completeness overall and in the general information (p=0.006, p=0.029; respectively). In pairwise comparisons, ChatGPT-5.3 showed significantly higher completeness than Perplexity (p=0.001, p=0.006; respectively). Completeness rates ranged 47%-64.3% overall, 46%-68.3% general information, 33.3%-50% diagnosis, and 48.3%-60.3% treatment. Readability differed significantly among the chatbots (p&lt;0.001). Based on mean scores, the ranking was ChatGPT-5.3&gt;Gemini=Copilot&gt;Perplexity. ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, and Copilot were easy, whereas Perplexity was moderately difficult.Conclusion: All chatbots showed similar accuracy, but ChatGPT-5.3 performed better in completeness and readability. Chatbots may be useful in Turkish patient education.

evidence_items.summary: Insurance claim analytics is often constrained by limited access to real-world data, which restricts the evaluation of advanced artificial intelligence approaches in practical insurance settings. Leveraging the SynthETIC framework, this study systematically evaluates classical actuarial models, neural-network-based methods, generative adversarial networks, and reinforcement learning for three core components of insurance claim processes: claim severity, incremental payments, and settlement delays. GAN-based data augmentation is implemented using task-specific architectures, including a tabular GAN for claim severity, an LSTM-based sequence GAN for incremental payments, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty for settlement delays, while Proximal Policy Optimization provides a sequential decision-learning framework for claim processes. Experimental results show that the performance of data-driven approaches is task-dependent, with GAN-based data augmentation improving some predictive measures but not consistently across all tasks and evaluation metrics. PPO-based reinforcement learning is more sensitive to task formulation and model design, reflecting the importance of action-space specification and reward structures. Additional experiments and mathematical analysis further examine the role of task-specific constraints in sequential payment allocation and delay prediction, highlighting the importance of admissible actions, state representation, and reward design. Overall, the findings illustrate how synthetic insurance environments can support the systematic evaluation of emerging AI paradigms and provide methodological insights into the task-dependent roles of GAN-based data augmentation and reinforcement learning in insurance claim analytics.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Insurance Claim Analytics in Synthetic Environments

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides excellent resolution at the cost of shallow penetration, limiting its ability for plaque burden (PB) assessment. A deep learning (DL) algorithm was therefore developed to provide fully automated assessment of PB and vessel size from OCT. Objectives We aimed to perform a head-to-head comparison of AI-powered OCT versus intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) for PB quantification, using histopathology as the reference standard. Methods Ten post-mortem human hearts were harvested. All the 29 major epicardial coronary arteries were perfused and underwent OCT and IVUS pullbacks. After imaging, the arteries were serially sectioned at 1-mm intervals for histopathology. Lumen and vessel contours were derived fully automatically from OCT using the DL algorithm and semi-automatically from IVUS. Histopathological measurements were obtained by experienced analysts. Statistical analyses accounted for within-patient clustering. Results A total of 852 paired OCT-IVUS-histopathology cross-sections were obtained. AI-powered OCT showed strong correlations with histopathology for the assessment of lumen area (r=0.89 [95% CI: 0.88–0.91]), vessel area (r=0.85 [95% CI: 0.83–0.87]), and PB (r=0.76 [95% CI: 0.73–0.79]). The corresponding correlations between IVUS and histopathology were 0.90 (95% CI: 0.89–0.92), 0.86 (95% CI: 0.84–0.88), and 0.79 (95% CI: 0.76–0.81), respectively. Comparisons of the OCT–histopathology and IVUS–histopathology correlation coefficients yielded p=0.336 for lumen area, p=0.444 for vessel area, and p=0.161 for PB. Both OCT and IVUS showed good diagnostic performance in identifying PB&gt;65%, with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve being 0.92 (95% CI: 0.90-0.94) and 0.92 (95% CI: 0.88-0.95), respectively.
evidence_items.title: AI-powered OCT shows similar performance to IVUS for plaque burden quantification: Head-to-head benchmark study against histopathology of native coronary arteries

evidence_items.summary: How large language models affect various social activities has been widely discussed; however, how large language models themselves influence the mechanisms of scientific knowledge production remains unclear. To investigate this question, this paper designs a quasi-experimental study based on a large-scale bibliometric dataset. Using a Difference-in-Differences model and analyzing citation records from 64,841 articles across 120 communication journals, we find that the emergence of large language models is associated with a widening of the visibility gap between Open Access (OA) and non-OA articles. Specifically, OA articles experienced a significant post-ChatGPT citation acceleration of approximately 0.84% per month, accumulating to roughly 10% over 12 months. Importantly, this estimate represents a conservative lower bound, as gradual LLM adoption and journal review lags attenuate the measured treatment intensity. The findings are consistent with the view that, while LLMs may promote knowledge dissemination, they also risk exacerbating inequality in academic knowledge production—though the precise mechanism behind this pattern remains an important direction for future research.
evidence_items.title: Do LLMs Read for Free? Auditing the Open Access Bias in AI-Mediated Science

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large language models have intensified public debate about the role of AI in supporting research pipelines, from hypothesis generation to experimental planning, execution, communication, and evaluation. While pattern recognition and automation improve efficiency, scholars are also raising deeper concerns about agency, creativity, intellectual ownership, and the potential erosion of human judgment in scientific work. This Special Interest Group (SIG) aims to create an open space for discussing emerging opportunities and challenges in AI-supported social computing research. We will discuss AI use across diverse research contexts, including individual inquiry, team formation and collaboration, peer review of papers and proposals, interdisciplinary knowledge production, and governance. We will also address the responsible design of AI systems that support deeper insights with greater confidence, promote new team collaboration and trust, and intentionally introduce productive frictions that cultivate critical and creative thinking. By bringing together scholars from HCI, AI, the social sciences, and related fields, this SIG will develop a shared blueprint for an AI-empowered social computing research agenda. More importantly, it will create a space for researchers to revisit their values, reaffirm human-centered commitments, and promote resilience in an ever-evolving AI era.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Social Computing Research in the Age of AI: Agency, Collaboration, and Governance

evidence_items.summary: We present CollabPEAS, a collaborative system for artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in which pairs of learners come to understand how an AI agent’s behavior is produced by human specification. Working in shared virtual reality (VR), learners jointly specify a virtual cleaning robot using the PEAS framework (Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors), developing competencies for reasoning about how AI agents sense, decide, and act. The system integrates three coordinated design elements: (1) a five-step PEAS-guided design flow, implemented in VR, that makes agent specification choices spatially grounded and observable, (2) a block-based coding interface that preserves the perceive, decide, act reasoning cycle, and (3) collaboration supports designed to structure negotiation and shared ownership between partners. We situate CollabPEAS within AI literacy and collaborative learning research and discuss directions for future evaluation.
evidence_items.title: CollabPEAS: A Collaborative VR System for Learning AI Agent Design Through the PEAS Framework

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly embedded in software development workflows. Since the Greenland Crisis of early 2026, there has been a renewed push for evaluation of European reliance on American tech. The concern over American GenAI tools is particularly relevant in Denmark who was in the direct line of fire during the geopolitical tension escalation. Through questionnaires (N=13) and interviews (N=12) with software developers, we examine how developers reflect on the GenAI tools they are using, how geopolitical tensions inform GenAI tool usage, and who is responsible for selecting GenAI tools. Our findings show that American GenAI acceptance has wavered with multiple developers actively seeking alternatives to American tech while others raised concerns about a lack of European alternatives as a main barrier for change. Our study provides an important snapshot in time, of how political tension affects collaborative technologies on the ground while reinforcing AI sovereignty as a future avenue of research.
evidence_items.title: ?The damage has been done?: AI Diplomacy and the Impact of Geopolitical Tensions on AI Tool Acceptance in Denmark in Q1 2026

evidence_items.summary: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) techniques into groundwater quality assessments is a pivotal step toward achieving water resource sustainability and ensuring its safety for human consumption. This is achieved by leveraging the advanced analytical capabilities of these technologies. Parameters such as pH, total dissolved solids (TDS), total alkalinity (T.A), chloride, sulfate (SO4), phosphorus oxide (PO4), Temperature (T) , electrical conductivity(EC), turbidity (Tur), bicarbonate (HCO3), total hardness (T.H), calcium hardness (Ca.H), magnesium hardness (Mg.H), sodium (Na), potassium (K) , and dissolved oxygen were analyzed to assess groundwater quality in Duhok City, Iraq. Water Quality Index (WQI) and Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System for Drinking (ANFIS-D) were employed in classifying water quality as excellent, good, poor, very poor, and unsuitable. It is beneficial to infer water quality for the individuals and decision-makers in the region. The WQI and ANFIS-D of the research area are between (37-50) (33-49), respectively. The overall WQI of the research area finds that the groundwater is safe and potable. The statistical metrics such as root mean square error (RMSE), mean bias error (MBE), and correlation coefficient (R) are used to check the validity of the ANFIS-D model. Studies show that the R value, MBE, and RMSE of the ANFIS-D model are (0.851, 2.9 and 3.81) respectively. Based on the results of these Statistical parameters, the ANFIS-D estimation model can predict the groundwater quality index of Duhok City with reasonable accuracy, which is useful and valuable for estimating the groundwater quality index.
evidence_items.title: EVALUATING POTABILITY OF GROUNDWATER USING AI-DRIVEN APPROACHES

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates how voice agent (VA) response styles and task cognitive levels affect users’ information processing performance and satisfaction in voice user interface environments. Prior research focused primarily on response length or naturalness, leaving a gap in how information structuring influences objective performance across task difficulty levels. We conducted a 3×3 Latin Square experiment with 30 participants, manipulating response style (Narrative, Enumerative, Categorical) and cognitive level (Recall, Understand, Analyze). Using ART-ANOVA and LMM as a robustness check, we found that the Style × Cognitive Level interaction was significant for performance in both analyses (ART: p=.020; LMM: p=.026) but non-significant for satisfaction. This asymmetry suggests a performance–satisfaction discrepancy that we refer to as “User Illusion,” further supported by a significant Style × Cog interaction on the normalized Gap (ART: p=.035; LMM: borderline). These findings indicate that VA response design must dynamically adapt to task cognitive level, integrating both objective and subjective evaluation metrics.
evidence_items.title: Beyond User Illusions: An Analysis of the Relationship Between Subjective Satisfaction and Objective Performance in Voice Agent Interaction

evidence_items.summary: This SIG will provide CSCW, HCI, XR, AI, and learning sciences researchers and practitioners with an opportunity to discuss how AI can support collaboration in XR-based professional training. Prior work has explored XR for simulation-based training and AI for tutoring, feedback, assessment, and adaptive learning. However, while AI is often discussed as an interactive partner or agent, less attention has been paid to how AI can support collaboration among human trainees in XR-based team training. In professional training contexts such as healthcare, emergency response, education, manufacturing, and workplace learning, AI agents may act as tutors, patients, victims, clients, coaches, evaluators, or facilitators, shaping how trainees communicate, coordinate, make decisions, and reflect on their performance. This SIG will create a space to discuss how these AI roles should be designed, how learners and instructors interact with AI-supported XR training systems, what methods are needed to study collaborative learning and teamwork in these settings, and what ethical, pedagogical, and deployment challenges should guide future CSCW research on AI-supported immersive team training.
evidence_items.title: From Individual Guidance to Team Support: AI in XR Professional Training

evidence_items.summary: Poultry not only provides good animal protein but also provides a source of livelihood and economic growth for individuals and society. Poultry production is threatened by coccidiosis caused by Eimeria species. The aim of this study was to evaluate in vitro oocysticidal activities of Vernonia amygdalina (VA) leaf extract and its fractions. Sporulation inhibition bioassay was used to evaluate the activity of the crude methanol extract and its solvent (n-hexane, ethyl acetate and methanol) fractions on sporulation of Eimeria oocysts. The extract and fractions were subjected to phytochemical analysis. Oral inoculation of the experimental broiler birds with oocysts was used to determine the specie of Eimeria through postmortem examination. VA extract and fractions were administered in concentrations of 0.1; 0.2 and 0.4 mg/ml in a Mcmaster culture chamber of concentrated sporulating oocysts under microscopic observation. Amprolium (0.1; 0.2 and 0.4 mg/ml), was used as control. Crude extract showed high levels of terpenoids and alkaloids, moderate concentrations of saponins, reducing sugars, total phenolics and steroids; ethyl acetate fraction had high concentration of terpenoids, moderate concentration of total phenolics, reducing sugars, saponins and alkaloids; n-hexane fraction had high concentration of steroids and terpenoids, moderate concentration of tannins, reducing sugar and alkaloids, while methanol fraction showed steroids, total phenolics, reducing sugars and saponins in moderate concentration. Postmortem examination of dead birds showed lesions consistent with Eimeria tenella infection. Oocysticidal activity was evidenced by lack of sporulation of oocysts when fractions were mixed with oocysts in the Mcmaster chamber slide. The highest oocysticidal activity (62.67 %) was recorded with ethyl acetate fraction. These results provide evidence for the use of VA as a preventive agent against coccidiosis, and as feed additive in the control of coccidiosis.
evidence_items.title: In Vitro Oocysticidal Effect of Vernonia amygdalina Del, Leaf Extract and Fractions on Sporulating Eimeria tenella Oocysts

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming cardiac electrophysiology (EP) by enabling automated interpretation of electrocardiograms, intracardiac electrograms, wearable sensor data, and imaging modalities. These technologies promise improved diagnostic accuracy, procedural efficiency, and personalized risk stratification across a wide spectrum of arrhythmia care. However, the integration of AI into clinical EP raises important ethical, practical, and regulatory concerns. Many current models function as opaque systems with limited explainability, while training datasets often lack adequate representation across sex, race, geography, and socioeconomic status. These limitations raise the risk of biased performance, reduced generalizability, and erosion of clinician trust. Furthermore, cost, infrastructure requirements, and regulatory complexity threaten equitable global adoption. This review examines the ethical foundations of AI in electrophysiology, focusing on dataset bias, fairness, explainability, and accountability. We discuss the clinical consequences of black box models, outline strategies to improve transparency, and explore emerging regulatory and legal frameworks. Finally, we highlight future horizons including digital twins, multimodal risk engines, and real time procedural guidance systems. Responsible deployment of AI in EP will require rigorous validation, continuous monitoring, clinician oversight, and intentional efforts to ensure equitable access across diverse populations.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiac Electrophysiology Ethics, Explainability, Equity, and the Road Ahead.

evidence_items.summary: Cross-species integration of single-cell transcriptomes requires establishing gene correspondences to enable comparative analysis of expression profiles across organisms. Current approaches predominantly rely on Ensembl homology tables; although gene-family expansion and contraction can reflect biologically meaningful evolutionary divergence, default many-to-many mappings can overweight expanded gene-family signals during integration and generate mapping-associated microclusters that lack clear cell-type identity, thereby complicating direct cell-type alignment. Although restricting mappings to a one-to-one scheme suppresses such artifacts, it reduces the number of homology gene pairs by ∼8% (about 900 pairs). To address this limitation, we develop a protein large language model (pLLM)–based gene homology mapping strategy that boosts the number of homology gene pairs. By enforcing a one-to-one mapping constraint and integrating pLLM-derived representations with sequence similarity, we construct a fused mapping approach, which achieves top performance in a comprehensive benchmark based on a curated cross-species atlas spanning nine data sets, 11 species, and more than 3.2 million cells. Our method further identifies previously unannotated cell-type marker pairs, facilitating novel cross-species marker discovery. These results establish a robust framework for gene homology mapping in cross-species transcriptome integration, improving both accuracy and biological interpretability.
evidence_items.title: Protein large language model–assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration

evidence_items.summary: T he rapid development of large language models, or LLMs, has created new opportunities to reconsider how instructors approach time-intensive tasks, such as grading and feedback. Naidu et al. provide a timely examination of this application in undergraduate biology education through their evaluation of LLM-based grading using authentic student work (1). The study moves discussion of artificial intelligence in assessment beyond speculation and toward practical evaluation. Rather than suggest­ ing that LLMs should replace instructor judgment, the authors provide a foundation for examining how these technologies may complement human assessment. Their approach is also notable for its low financial and technological barrier to entry. Naidu et al. evaluated ChatGPT GPT 4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash using 200 essays from an introductory biology course (1). The models assessed student work with a standardized rubric under zero shot and few shot prompting conditions, and their scores were compared with those of a trained human grader. Agreement varied by model, prompting method, and rubric component. Performance was strongest for writing-related criteria and more variable for scientific content, reflection, ethi­ cal reasoning, and policy development. The models also differed from one another, demonstrating that conclusions about AI grading cannot necessarily be generalized from a single LLM (1). Several features strengthen the study. The use of authentic student writing gives the investigation greater educational relevance than studies based on artificial or highly constrained responses. Evaluating several contemporary LLMs is also important because models may interpret the same assessment task differently. Saez et al. similarly found meaningful variation when comparing six LLMs used for grading in higher education (2). Together, these findings suggest that AI-based assessment should consider not only whether LLMs can grade student work, but also which models, prompts, rubrics, and assessment types produce reliable results.
evidence_items.title: Expanding the role of large language models in biology assessment

evidence_items.summary: Cardiac arrest can cause catastrophic brain injury manifested as coma and is a leading cause of death. Among patients with poor neurological outcomes, further stratification distinguishing brain death from severe disability is critical for guiding goals-of-care decisions and resource allocation. Additionally, the Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) score provides a granular assessment of neurological function in comatose patients. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based approach to classify brain death and predict the FOUR score and its individual components (eye response, motor response, brainstem reflexes, and respiration) using structured clinical registry data from the Yale Multimodal Outcome CHAracterization (MOCHA) registry. Each patient record comprised structured data including demographics, comorbidities, arrest characteristics, neurological examinations (Glasgow Coma Scale), laboratory values, electroencephalography, and neuroimaging categorical findings. The complete Yale MOCHA registry included 1,032 post-cardiac arrest patients. For the primary brain death classification experiment, we constructed a balanced cohort of 200 patients consisting of 100 brain death-positive and 100 brain-death-negative cases, divided into 120 patients for training, 40 for validation, and 40 for testing. We evaluated LLaMA-3.2-3B and Qwen3-4B as frozen feature extractors with lightweight multi-layer perceptron prediction heads. Qwen3-4B achieved the best brain death classification performance, with an AUC-ROC of 0.787, balanced accuracy of 0.775, sensitivity of 0.650, and specificity of 0.900, compared with an AUC-ROC of 0.752 and balanced accuracy of 0.725 for LLaMA-3.2-3B. For FOUR score prediction, Qwen3-4B and LLaMA-3.2-3B achieved mean absolute errors of 2.446 and 2.536 points, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-based brain death classification and FOUR score prediction in post-cardiac arrest patients using structured clinical registry data

evidence_items.summary: Objective To compare ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, and DeepSeek-R1 in assigning main Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS) categories from findings-only coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) reports and to characterize management-relevant classification errors. Methods This retrospective diagnostic-accuracy study included 2,100 category-balanced findings-only CCTA reports (300 per CAD-RADS category). Two experienced CCTA radiologists graded the English-translated reports; 12 disagreements were resolved by a third. ChatGPT-4o was evaluated in standard mode, ChatGPT-5 in Thinking mode, and DeepSeek-R1 in Deep Thinking mode; model generation and inference mode therefore varied together. Exact-match accuracy with 95% Wilson confidence intervals (CIs), paired comparisons, and unweighted Gwet AC1 with 95% CIs were calculated. Management-relevant transitions and digital subtraction angiography (DSA) findings among high-risk downgrades were analyzed. Results DeepSeek-R1 had an exact-match accuracy of 82.57% (95% CI, 80.89–84.13) and AC1 of 0.797 (95% CI, 0.778–0.816). ChatGPT-5 had an accuracy of 80.19% (95% CI, 78.43–81.84) and AC1 of 0.769 (95% CI, 0.749–0.789), whereas ChatGPT-4o had an accuracy of 53.62% (95% CI, 51.48–55.74) and AC1 of 0.460 (95% CI, 0.435–0.485). Cochran's Q test was significant (Q = 657.87; df = 2; P &lt; 0.001); after Holm correction, DeepSeek-R1 also outperformed ChatGPT-5 in the paired comparison ( P = 0.026), and both outperformed ChatGPT-4o (both P &lt; 0.001). ChatGPT-4o downgraded 127/900 (14.11%) reference high-risk reports to CAD-RADS 3 or lower. Of these 127 cases, 65 underwent DSA within three months; DSA supported the original high-risk assessment in 56/65 (86.15%). The corresponding high-risk downgrade proportions were 37/900 (4.11%) for ChatGPT-5 and 23/900 (2.56%) for DeepSeek-R1.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-assisted CAD-RADS classification: structured report extraction, accuracy, and clinical decision-making risk of ChatGPT-4o/5 and DeepSeek-R1

evidence_items.summary: We present ShapeLib , the first method that uses the priors of Large Language Models (LLMs) to design libraries of programmatic 3D shape abstractions. Our system accepts two forms of user-provided design intent: high-level text descriptions of functions to include in the output library and a small seed set of exemplar shapes. We discover a library of abstractions that matches this design intent with a guided LLM workflow that first proposes different ways of applying and implementing functions, and then validates these functions are helpful in representing seed set shapes. To extend beyond the seed set, we develop library-specific recognition networks that map shapes (represented as primitives, voxels, or point clouds) to programs that use these newly discovered abstractions. Across multiple modeling domains (split by shape category), we find that LLMs, when thoughtfully combined with geometric reasoning, can be guided to author libraries of abstraction functions that generalize across shape distributions. Our framework takes a step towards realizing the long-standing shape analysis aspiration of discovering reusable, programmatic shape abstractions while exposing interpretable, semantically aligned interfaces. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that ShapeLib provides distinct advantages over prior alternative abstraction discovery works in terms of generalization, usability, and maintaining plausibility under manipulation. Finally, we demonstrate that ShapeLib’s abstraction functions unlock a number of downstream applications, combining LLM reasoning over shape programs with geometry processing tools to support shape editing and generation workflows.
evidence_items.title: ShapeLib: Designing a library of programmatic 3D shape abstractions with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significant potential in healthcare, such as automating routine tasks and supporting complex decision-making processes. In fields like oncology, LLMs can extract and organize unstructured patient data, streamlining workflows and supporting imaging or clinical evaluations. This information can then be integrated into predictive models, enhancing patient prognosis assessments. However, deploying LLMs poses challenges, some of which are related to their performance variability due to the inherent probabilistic nature of LLMs, prompt differences, and software updates, which may lead to inconsistent outcomes. Even with identical prompts and contexts, LLMs can exhibit variability. It is essential to rigorously evaluate the clinical accuracy and reproducible outcomes of the LLM for clinical data extraction in clinical settings for AI decision support tools and clinical use. Reliable information retrieval requires consistent LLM behavior. The study of the LLMs variability and its effect on clinical AI decision support tools will be presented and discussed.
evidence_items.title: Reliability of large language models for clinical data extraction in AI decision support tools

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model–based chatbots (LLM-CBs) are increasingly used as mental health support tools. Risks and harms are discussed especially for unsupervised use and for vulnerable groups. A naturalistic characterization of the use of LLM-CBs by patients with mental health disorders is currently lacking. Objective The goal of this cross-sectional study is to investigate demographic and clinical characteristics of users of LLM-CB for mental health and their associations with use behavior. Methods Across 6 months, qualitative and quantitative data on LLM-CB use for mental health were collected in a consecutive sample of psychotherapy outpatients in routine treatment with at least 1 diagnosed mental health disorder. Results are reported descriptively and supported by exploratory inferential analyses. Results Within a total of 812 included outpatients who reported on LLM-CB use for mental health, 245 (30.1%) reported having used LLM-CBs for mental health (once: 69/217, 31.8%; weekly: 118/217, 54.4%; and daily: 30/217, 13.8%). Users were more likely to be younger, female, better educated, students, or unemployed. In total, 61.4% (121/197) have used LLM-CBs in self-reported personal crisis situations, of whom, 67.7% (82/121) found the experience unhelpful. LLM-CB use showed a weak, imprecise association with the number of diagnoses in the included diagnosis groups and was higher for anxiety and eating disorder diagnoses and lower for somatoform disorders. Post hoc multivariable analyses suggest that higher use in eating disorders and lower use in somatoform disorders were attenuated after adjusting for age, while higher use for anxiety disorders persisted. LLM-CBs were generally evaluated positively across various dimensions, especially when self-reported personal crisis situation use was experienced as helpful.
evidence_items.title: Use of Generic Large Language Model Chatbots for Mental Health Issues Among Patients Seeking Psychotherapy: Cross-Sectional Mixed Methods Analysis in a German University Hospital Outpatient Clinic

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The peer‐review process in economics faces two well‐documented challenges: a shortage of willing referees, and prolonged turnaround times. We examine whether large language models (LLMs) can help to address these inefficiencies without introducing systematic bias, using two pre‐registered experiments across four LLMs, and over 29,000 evaluations of 1220 anonymized papers. LLMs reliably differentiate research quality by journal rank, and ratings are positively correlated with realized citation impact. However, model performance varies substantially: GPT and Gemma show the strongest evaluative gradients, while LLaMA assigns the maximum score to 81% of papers, rendering it uninformative for quality discrimination. GPT excels at detecting AI‐generated content; Claude‐generated papers receive the highest quality ratings and are the hardest to detect. Varying author identity in the second experiment reveals that three of the four LLMs assign significantly higher ratings to papers attributed to prominent economists and elite Western institutions, and lower ratings to papers with non‐Western affiliations, mirroring the prestige gradients documented in the human peer‐review literature. These biases persist when paper quality is held constant, highlighting the necessity for author‐blind inputs for any editorial deployment of LLM‐assisted screening.
evidence_items.title: Large language models and human judgement in scientific peer review: evidence from over 1000 published economics papers

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To assess the anatomic evaluation performance of the uterine artery (UA) on routine multiphase abdominopelvic CT images, and to investigate whether artificial intelligence iterative reconstruction (AIIR) can improve this performance to a level comparable to that on CTA images. Methods: This retrospective study included 50 patients who underwent multiphase abdominopelvic CT. Aarterial phase (AP) images were reconstructed with AIIR (group B) in addition to the routine hybrid iterative reconstruction (HIR) (group A). Another 50 patients who underwent routine abdominal aorta CTA were retrospectively identified, and their images were reconstructed with HIR (group C). The anatomic evaluation performance of UA in terms of the interpretability of origins, branching pattern, and lumen diameter was compared across the 3 image sets. The objective image quality was also compared. Results: A total of 100 patients (age 18 to 65 y) were investigated, and 300 UAs were evaluated (150 images × 2 UAs). Both group B and group C outperformed group A in terms of the proportion of UAs with identifiable origins (90% and 88% vs. 68%), classifiable branching pattern (89% and 87% vs. 71%), and totally measurable diameter (63% and 67% vs. 33%) (all P <0.017). No significant differences were found between groups B and C for any of these proportions (all P >0.017). The measured diameters exhibited excellent intraobserver agreement with ICC values of 0.90, 0.93, and 0.98 for groups A, B, and C, respectively. The UA attenuation was highest in group C, followed by group B and group A (all P <0.017). Group B exhibited the lowest noise in all scenarios (all P <0.017). No significant difference was found in the CNR of UA between group B and group C (all P >0.017). Sensitivity analysis excluding hypertensive patients confirmed the stability of the results. Conclusions: Anatomic evaluation performance of UA on routine multiphase abdominopelvic CT images is suboptimal.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Iterative Reconstruction in Multiphase Abdominopelvic CT: Added Value for Anatomic Evaluation of Uterine Artery

evidence_items.summary: This methodological study evaluated and compared the content quality and appropriateness of nursing care plans developed by nurses and artificial intelligence (AI) for addressing the psychosocial problems of patients with stomas. Two nursing care plans addressing the psychosocial needs of a patient with a stoma were developed: 1 generated by nurses and 1 generated by an AI system. The content quality and appropriateness of the care plans were independently evaluated by 12 experts, including nursing academics and clinical nurses, using the DISCERN measurement tool. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The mean DISCERN score of the nurse-generated care plan was significantly higher than that of the AI-generated care plan ( P =.008). Inter-rater agreement demonstrated good agreement. The findings indicate that nurse-generated care plans demonstrate superior content quality and overall integrity compared to AI-generated plans. AI-generated care plans exhibit potential as supportive tools in nursing care planning.
evidence_items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Into Nursing Care Planning

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) generally defines intelligence as an optimal association between input features and predictive behavior. In essence, it is defined as knowledge updating under adaptation, describing the static relationship between input features and decision accuracy in a human-interpretable form. This definition is not suitable for the cutting-edge colony of AI frameworks where intelligence evolves from fast, detailed, and organized learner AI agents. This paper introduces an innovative Human Gradient Artificial Intelligence (HGAI) approach to model intelligence as a measurable continuous gradient of knowledge updating under evolution with human-inspired behaviors such as metacognition-driven self-assessment, self-regulation, and self-reflection. In HGAI, pretrained machine learning models define AI agents to understand their evolutionary behavior by modeling gradient of knowledge updating with softmax probability, cross-entropy, stochastic gradient descent and regularization, while considering predictive performance over two phases of discrete time-steps. AI agents are also pretrained in the principal component basis of the original feature space. Additionally, confidence evolution over gradient is defined as an aggregated effect of high probabilities of predictions and the prediction losses to reflect metacognition-driven self-assessment. Trustability of knowledge update is also defined with the rolling statistics of losses and prior updated knowledge to integrate self-regulation and self-reflection. Experimental results of kernel-SVM, ridge-regression, Lasso, and Perceptron models, integrating fast, detailed, and organized learner AI agents with Digits and Fashion-MNIST datasets, show prediction accuracy in the second phases are generally higher (92-99%) for the fast and detailed learners. However, it is lower for the organized learners, satisfying higher accuracy in the second phase than in the first.
evidence_items.title: Human gradient artificial intelligence for self-aware learning systems

organizations: NCI, All India Institute of Medical Sciences

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly explored as clinical decision support tools, but their accuracy and applicability remain insufficiently evaluated. We therefore evaluated and compared the accuracy, completeness, readability, and real-world applicability of four AI chatbots in generating treatment plans for Paediatric Pulmonology Intensive care and Emergency cases.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of artificial intelligence chatbots for generating management plans in paediatric intensive care and pulmonology cases: A comparative study

evidence_items.summary: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is currently constrained by long scan times, limiting patient throughput and accessibility. Artificial Intelligence (AI) models have shown promise to make scans faster, therefore increasing patient throughput. However, simply increasing scan volume creates a secondary bottleneck: the finite capacity of radiologists to interpret a growing influx of data. To address this dual challenge, we propose a framework that integrates longitudinal imaging data to achieve significantly shorter scan times than current state-of-the-art methods. To streamline the resulting workload, we propose to leverage vast adult normative datasets to develop brain MRI foundation models that learn robust representations by leveraging domain-informed pretext tasks in which the training labels are easy to obtain, such as voxel-level brain age and Fazekas score predictions. This model will serve as a robust platform to automate, expedite, and enhance the precision of brain MRI analysis, ultimately bridging the gap between rapid data acquisition and actionable clinical insights. In this paper, we show examples of longitudinal MRI reconstruction that achieve up to 20× acceleration, adaptation of reconstruction models trained on adults to infants, voxel-level brain age prediction, and Fazekas score prediction.
evidence_items.title: Addressing inefficiencies in brain magnetic resonance imaging workflows with artificial intelligence

organizations: Duke University, Durham, NC, USA

evidence_items.summary: Objective: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) assistance on examination efficiency and ergonomics during cardiac sonography. Materials and Methods: Randomized, cross-over study design was used with an ultrasound equipment system, cardiovascular software, and integrated AI features. A cohort of experienced sonographers (N = 30) performed standardized examinations with and without AI features enabled. All participating sonographers were new equipment users. Metrics of timing with and without AI assistance were acquired. Movements of the non-scanning hand were recorded during a subset of studies to assess time spent in a predefined ergonomic zone. Results: Artificial intelligence assistance reduced mean examination time by 10.16 ± 0.95 minutes (95% CI, 12.10-8.22; P < .001) independent of experience, age, scanning sequence, or prior AI familiarity. A sub-analysis of hand motion during sonography (n = 9) found AI assistance reduced average distance traveled by 50% (47.9 m) compared with unassisted examinations (SD, 10.6; 95% CI, 39.74-55.97, P < .01). Conclusion: In this cohort of users, AI-assisted cardiac sonography significantly reduced acquisition time and increased time spent within their optimal hand reach. This kind of upgrade may help lower the risk of work-related musculoskeletal injuries in cardiac sonographers. Further studies, based on actual clinical settings, would help to further clarify these benefits.
evidence_items.title: Assessing the Efficiency and Ergonomic Benefits of Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Acquisition

evidence_items.summary: The metaverse connects immersive interfaces, virtual environments, artificial intelligence, extended reality, cloud and edge computing, digital twins, communication networks, and blockchain-based services. These technologies can support education, entertainment, commerce, training, and digital ownership, but they also create a broad, evolving cybersecurity surface. Identity theft, privacy loss, abnormal network activity, deepfake-based impersonation, and digital-asset fraud can occur across interconnected layers. This paper presents an independently written, student-oriented study of AI-assisted cybersecurity for the metaverse. It focuses on intelligent authentication, AI-based intrusion detection, privacy-aware learning, and protection of blockchain and NFT ecosystems. The paper describes a layered framework in which relevant security data are collected, processed with suitable AI methods, converted into risk decisions, and followed by proportionate responses. The study also discusses data quality, latency, interoperability, privacy, model attacks, and the need for human oversight. The central view is that AI should complement established cybersecurity controls rather than replace them.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Cybersecurity for the Metaverse: Research Challenges and Opportunities

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sachet water has become the primary source of potable water for many Nigerian households because of its affordability and widespread availability. However, inadequate compliance with production standards has compromised progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals by increasing the risk of microbial and chemical contamination. This review evaluates sachet water production practices, contamination sources, associated public health risks, and the effectiveness of regulatory agencies responsible for quality control. The study followed the PRISMA guidelines and employed a Boolean search strategy to synthesize evidence from published literature. A comparative assessment of drinking water sources, including well water, stored water, rainwater, surface water, bottled water, and sachet water, was conducted. The findings revealed the presence of heavy metals such as mercury, arsenic, nickel, lead, cadmium, chromium, iron, and manganese in several drinking water sources. Although bottled water was generally safer, prolonged exposure to sunlight promoted chemical leaching. Microbial contaminants, including total coliforms, fecal coliforms, and Escherichia coli , were detected in most water sources except bottled water. Exposure to heavy metals and microplastics may increase the risk of chronic diseases, while residues of antibiotics such as ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, and tetracycline may contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Integrating Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and artificial intelligence into water quality monitoring, alongside improved infrastructure and stronger regulatory enforcement, could enhance sachet water safety and reduce dependence on packaged water, particularly in underserved communities.
evidence_items.title: Contamination of Nigeria drinking water: A systematic review of public health implications
Overcoming the Curse of Dimensionality in Parabolic PDEs: A Monte Carlo-Neural Surrogate Framework with Benchmark Analysis

organizations: College of Economics, Hunan Agriculture University
evidence_items.summary: Microplastics (MPs) have transitioned from a predominantly marine concern to a defining threat facing terrestrial agroecosystems, where croplands now function as one of the largest global reservoirs of plastic particles. This review synthesizes evidence to construct an integrated narrative that links the entry of MPs into farmland with declining plant productivity, quantifiable economic losses, and the erosion of agricultural supply chain resilience. The synthesis is based on a documented search of Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar covering January 2018 to March 2026, with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria reported in Section 1.1. Sources, fate and soil-phase processes are treated in condensed form, because they are already covered comprehensively elsewhere; we retain only the evidence that propagates into crop, economic and supply-chain outcomes. Building on these soil-level disturbances, we evaluate the phytotoxic consequences for crops, spanning inhibited germination, impaired root architecture, reduced photosynthetic efficiency, disrupted nutrient acquisition, and the uptake and translocation of nano-sized particles into edible tissues. A central contribution of this review is the explicit coupling of these biophysical impacts to their economic and systemic dimensions, because recent global meta-analyses estimate that MP-induced photosynthetic suppression alone may reduce staple crop production by tens to hundreds of millions of tons annually, translating into substantial revenue losses, quality downgrading, remediation expenditure, and heightened exposure of food supply chains to shocks. Rather than reporting these modelled outputs at face value, we dissect the inferential chain that produces them, from effect size to biomass to harvestable yield to price, and we identify the assumptions at each step that determine whether the resulting figures are decision-grade.
evidence_items.title: Microplastic contamination in agricultural systems: impacts on plant productivity, economic losses, and supply chain resilience

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Touching the border of the world-famous “ Esophageal Cancer Belt ” the Kashmir Valley has a high burden of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). The contribution of environmental exposures remains largely inconclusive. Horticulture and agriculture are considered the backbone of the Kashmir economy; however, such practices have raised concerns regarding the potential environmental toxic metal accumulation due to excessive use of pesticides, fungicides, insecticides and fertilizers. This study evaluated the distribution pattern of selected trace elements in the environment and staple food items across the Valley. Methods A total of 117 samples comprising soil (n = 30), drinking water (n = 30), collard greens (n = 30), and paddy/rice (n = 27) were collected across all 10 districts of the Kashmir Valley in this descriptive-analytical study. The samples were analysed for trace elements—zinc (Zn), selenium (Se), copper (Cu), lead (Pb), chromium (Cr), barium (Ba), cadmium (Cd), arsenic (As), and cobalt (Co)—using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Median and percentile measures were used for estimating elemental contamination. Differences across sample types and districts were assessed using Kruskal–Wallis tests and Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Spearman correlation and principal component analysis were used to assess inter-element associations and multivariate patterns. Results Trace-element concentrations varied significantly across the samples for all 9 elements (FDR-adjusted P < 0.001). Soil demonstrated high median concentrations of Zn (244.0 ppm), Cu (110.75ppm), Pb (108.4ppm), Cr (114.5ppm), Ba (396.0 ppm), Cd (12.25ppm), and As (133.0ppm). All soil samples exceeded the applied reference values for As and Cd, while 83.3%, 70.0%, and 70.0% exceeded those for Cr, Cu, and Pb, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Tracing agrochemical footprints: heavy‑metal contamination and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma Risk in Kashmir- the northernmost state of India

organizations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Incheon National University, Incheon 22012, Republic of Korea

evidence_items.summary: Water utilities increasingly manage residual chlorine, conductivity, turbidity and water temperature in district metered areas (DMAs) from continuous on-line analyzers rather than from grab samples. Every decision that follows, from adjusting booster chlorination to ordering a flush or sending a crew, assumes that the analyzers are reporting the truth. In the Incheon network studied here, one year of hourly data from five DMAs contained a network-wide telemetry outage, water-temperature readings of up to 4913 °C, negative chlorine values and a turbidity channel frozen for 46 h, none of which the supervisory system had flagged. This paper asks whether such sensor and telemetry faults can be detected automatically, within the hour, at an alarm rate a control room will accept, using only the hourly data the utility already archives. Eleven unsupervised detectors from three families, statistical charts on the current reading or on time-series residuals (Hotelling T2, MEWMA, seasonal profile, VAR residual, dynamic PCA), general-purpose outlier detectors (Isolation Forest, one-class SVM, local outlier factor) and small neural networks (LSTM autoencoder, prediction-residual LSTM, a compact Transformer autoencoder), were run under one protocol and judged against the real faults and 900 injected faults of four types, with performance expressed as the operator sees it: events caught, hours to detection, and false alarms per week, counted both as alarm hours and as separate alarm episodes, with bootstrap intervals. Every family caught the real faults (seven events from three independent incidents) within the hour. They differed on the injected faults (recall 0.28–0.63) and above all on false alarms: the two LSTM models raised 0.5–0.8 alarm hours per DMA-week, and the current-reading control charts raised 9–10; counted as separate episodes, the spread was only 0.4–1.5.
evidence_items.title: Unsupervised Multivariate Anomaly Detection for Near-Real-Time Water-Quality Monitoring in District Metered Areas: A Three-Tier Benchmark Validated with Real-World Anomalies

organizations: Aichi Cancer Center Hospital

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Environmental monitoring of antineoplastic drug contamination has primarily focused on medication preparation areas and frequently touched surfaces. Consequently, contamination in nonpreparation areas and on infrequently touched surfaces, such as ceilings, remains poorly characterized. This study evaluated fluorouracil contamination on floors and ceilings in preparation and nonpreparation areas. Methods This study was conducted at Aichi Cancer Center, Japan. Samples were collected from floor and ceiling surfaces in the hospital pharmacy, outpatient chemotherapy center, and inpatient ward. Cleaning practices at the sampling sites were also assessed. Fluorouracil concentrations were measured using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. At the time of sampling, closed-system drug-transfer devices (CSTDs) were not used for fluorouracil preparation or administration. Results Fluorouracil was detected on all sampled floor and ceiling surfaces, including those in nonpreparation areas where antineoplastic drugs were not handled. The highest contamination levels were detected on the preparation room floor (3.104 ng/cm 2 ) and the pharmacy break room ceiling (2.440 ng/cm 2 ). In the outpatient chemotherapy center, relatively high contamination levels were detected on the nursing station floor (0.622 ng/cm 2 ) and nursing break room ceiling (0.419 ng/cm 2 ). Conclusions Fluorouracil contamination was detected in nonpreparation areas and on ceiling surfaces near air-conditioning units that were not routinely touched or cleaned. These findings suggest that contamination may spread through the movement of healthcare workers and materials and may accumulate on infrequently cleaned surfaces. As part of contamination control, the use of CSTDs may need to be implemented and environmental monitoring may need to be extended beyond medication preparation areas.
evidence_items.title: Environmental contamination with fluorouracil on floors and ceilings in antineoplastic drug preparation and nonpreparation areas of a Japanese cancer center
